newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africa truth body to say if ANC fought just war.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa truth body to say if ANC fought just war.

text.p: Archbishop Desmond Tutu, head of South Africa's truth commission, said on Friday almost everyone agreed apartheid was evil but the commission had yet to decide if the armed struggle against it had been justified.

Tutu, addressing a news conference after a meeting with leaders of the ruling African National Congress, urged members of the former liberation group to apply for amnesty along with the police and soldiers of the apartheid era.

"We indicated (in the meeting) that the commission is going to make, in its final report, its determination about morality in the broad sense, our decisions about whether this or that policy was morally justified," Tutu said.
He said the theory of a "just war" had to be tested against a range of criteria, including whether the party concerned had exhausted all other forms of resistance.
"Most of us have made a moral decision about apartheid, that was an evil policy," Tutu added.
ANC acting secretary-general Cheryl Carolus, who led the ANC delegation in the talks, told a separate news conference the meeting had clarified "misunderstandings" between the two sides.
"Our struggle against apartheid was what we regard as a just war...We thought it important to state that this would be our base assumption in responding to the questions of the commission," she said.
The commission has sent the ANC and other political organisations lists of questions on submissions the parties made last year on their role in apartheid and the fight against it.

The commission, set up to promote the healing of apartheid's wounds, can grant indemnity from prosecution to those who confess to crimes or human rights abuses committed on either side of the race war.
The ANC has said that because it was fighting a just war its members could not be placed in the same category as apartheid police officers and soldiers.
Tutu said commissioners and the ANC agreed on Friday that by applying for amnesty ANC members would not be accepting "moral equivalence" with those who enforced apartheid.

Alex Boraine, Tutu's deputy on the commission, added: "A party that claims that its cause was just has to accept responsibility for any abuses that may have taken place in the course of pursuing that struggle, which means applications for amnesty would have to be made by liberation forces."
Transport Minister Mac Maharaj, who was in the ANC delegation, predicted the commission's investigation would soon draw in top political leaders from the apartheid era.
"I think the truth process and the investigations have reached a critical point where nobody at the highest level will be left with a hiding place shortly," he said.
